extracted.intended_audience: lay readers interested in anatomy and natural theology (inexperienced in anatomy/mathematics)
extracted.subtask_description: An expository didactic treatment that uses anatomical structure and mechanical reasoning to argue for design in living bodies; intended to instruct readers with little prior anatomical knowledge by means of clear examples, figures, and plain mechanical analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting inexperienced readers with concise methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The demonstrations are collected for persons unexperienced and not habituated to heap up many lemmas; use the concise and easiest methods to render demonstrations intelligible to those with little mathematical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid long sequences of preliminary lemmas and verbose style; enlarge particulars only where necessary to convey the design plainly to the reader's apprehension; include clear figures and plain mechanical explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anatomical figures to give a handle to the unlearned
rubrics_metrics.description: Present muscles and bones 'as they lie upon a humane Body' (front and back figures) so that unexperienced persons can see structures and their relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide labelled plates/figures (e.g. Tab. VIII Fig. 1 & 2, Tab. IX) and refer to them when describing courses of fibres, insertions, and articulations; figures should accompany verbal descriptions to aid comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how muscles are adapted to their motions relative to tendons and joints
rubrics_metrics.description: Show how the arrangement and insertion of muscle fibres and tendons determine the motions they discharge with respect to bones and joints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concrete instances (deltoid, pectoral, latissimus dorsi, gastrocnemius) describing fixed and movable ends, directions of fibres, and resulting movements to demonstrate adaptation of form to function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize multiplicity and fineness of muscle fibres to avoid tear
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue that muscles are composed of an immense number of very fine fibres so that no single fibre bears a sensible part of load and fibres are not torn by violent motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify or illustrate that individual fibres are extremely small (smaller than a woman's hair) and that their large multiplicity distributes force; use this to support claims of durable, purposeful construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present muscles as composed of many small 'machines' to achieve velocity and nimbleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat each fibre or micro-component as a small mechanical element whose combined action yields rapid, nimble motions (e.g., fingers, tongue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mechanical metaphors to make the role of micro-structure intuitive; point to motions that require speed and dexterity as evidence of such organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue that displacement of individual fibres would cause confusion and harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim that among the innumerable fine fibres, none can be displaced without causing disorder or damage to the whole structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the sensitivity of complex fibre arrangements as an argument against random formation; illustrate by noting how delicate alignments produce precise function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quantitative mechanical estimates as evidence (force calculations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give mechanical estimates (e.g., deltoid fibres acting collectively equated to 35,680 pounds, and inability of the joined fibres to separate under great weight) as demonstration of extraordinary design and strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, supply numerical examples or thought-experiments showing forces and balances to bolster claims of remarkable capacity beyond random expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use course of fibres and insertions to explain function
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the precise course of muscle fibres and their points of attachment (e.g. deltoid fixed at shoulder, other end at bone tube near joint) to explain resulting motions (lifting arm, bending at shoulder, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include step-by-step descriptive examples for different muscles, indicating fixed vs movable insertions and the resulting lever actions; rely on anatomy texts (Borelli, Brookes) for authoritative descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive philosophical convictions from anatomical observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform anatomical facts (fine structure, arrangement, capabilities) into philosophical conclusions about wisdom and design, inviting sceptics to reflect on whether chance could produce such machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cumulative anatomical examples to produce a persuasive sequence leading readers to question purely chance-based explanations; emphasize scale and repetitiveness of organized parts as strong evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point out skull features that serve protective and developmental purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerate skull design features: hard casing to protect soft brain; skull made of several parts joined by sutures to allow mobility in childbirth and later ossification; holes for spinal cord and vessels; complex ear cavities for hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain each anatomical detail with its specific purpose (e.g., sutures for birthing mobility, later closure for protection) and relate to functional necessity rather than accidental form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight presence of orifices and cavities where function requires them
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that skull and facial bones contain openings placed where necessary (for medulla spinalis, blood-vessels, nasal air passage to aid sucking and breathing) indicating purposeful design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific examples (cheek-bone orifice allowing air through nose) to show that small cavities are not accidental but tailored to physiological needs; consider consequences if absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain backbone (vertebral column) design to balance protection and flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the backbone consists of many small vertebrae with central holes forming a hollow tube for the spinal marrow; small, numerous vertebrae allow gentle flexion without acute angles that would constrict the spinal cord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geometric analogy (inscribing polygons in a circle) to explain why many small pieces yield near-circular flexibility and avoid acute inflections; stress protection of spinal marrow as design constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe intervertebral cartilage functions (wear prevention, compressibility, elasticity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intervening cartilage between vertebrae prevents rubbing/wear, allows compression on the side of bending and extension on the other, and provides an elastic restoring force to return the column to its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail the three uses: 1) prevent vertebrae abrasion; 2) permit asymmetric approach/recession during bending; 3) supply elastic recoil after deformation. Cite Borelli's 'Artificium Structurae Spinae Dorsi' as mechanical appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples of joint specialization to show design for constrained motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that different joints (shoulder, hip, knee) have different shapes and attachments to permit necessary motions (e.g., thigh’s ball-and-socket allows multi-directional motion; knee is structured to bend forward/backward but not sideways).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe joint geometry, cartilage coverings, ligaments, and bands that secure joints while preserving freedom of motion; contrast functional differences between joints to show adaptive design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize ribs’ cartilaginous attachments for respiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Point out that ribs are attached by cartilage to the breast-bone to allow easier inflection during respiration and to employ elastic return after muscular action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the respiration example to show how cartilaginous composition is functionally appropriate; mention Borelli's mechanical discussion for power and action of ribs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for specialized features (hip bones, womb protection, fulcrum function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain that hip bones strengthen and protect the wombs of women and serve as immovable fulcrums supporting thighs, legs and feet when bearing the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connect morphological form to reproductive and locomotor functions; use this to argue multifunctional purposeful arrangement rather than chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe hollow bone architecture (strength with lightness and marrow storage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that some long bones (thigh-bone) are hollow to be hard and stiff enough to bear weight while light enough not to encumber motion, and to contain marrow necessary for bodily service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain trade-off between strength and weight, and the dual role of hollowness (mechanical advantage + marrow receptacle); point readers to common observations (thigh-bones found in charnel-houses) to inspect structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show joint surface design (cartilage, polished surfaces, bands) for smooth, secure motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Thigh-head surrounded by polished cartilage to reduce resistance and pain; the round head is fastened by a band (ligament) for steadiness yet allows motion; broad surrounding bands tie the joint while preserving freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail cartilage, ligaments, grooves and eminences (e.g., two heads at knee with groove between) showing how each micro-feature contributes to smooth, constrained motion and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain timing and adaptation of teeth eruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe that teeth are endowed with properties different from other bones and that they appear at stages (not in first months) suited to the infant's digestive capacity, indicating adaptive timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use developmental timing of dentition as evidence of functional adaptation; note how eruption corresponds to digestive readiness rather than accidental schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe embryonic bone formation sequence as complex and staged
rubrics_metrics.description: Report that bones of embryos arise from little fibres or threads (slimy) which become nervous, then cartilaginous, and finally ossify, with varying consistency across months — a gradual, non-trivial process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use embryological observations (Malpighi, Harvey) to argue that bone formation is a directed, developmental process requiring explanation beyond chance; highlight differences at stages and complexity of timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cross-disciplinary empirical evidence (chemistry, surgery) about bones and marrow
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite chemical distillation showing bones yield oil and watery parts (volatile salts), and surgical cautions that applying oil/moisture to bare bone causes corruption; use such empirical findings to support claims about bone composition and vulnerabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring in experimental chemistry and surgical practice as corroborating evidence for anatomical arguments (e.g., marrow composition, susceptibility to liquids); interpret scriptural metaphors (oil in bones) with surgical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign functional roles to marrow (lubrication, keeping ligaments supple, preventing cartilage attrition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue that marrow inhabits hollow bones to render limbs smooth and supple, prevent cartilage wear in joints, and maintain ligaments in proper condition — analogous to greasing axles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mechanical analogies (greased axletrees) to show necessity of marrow; describe consequences of dryness (brittleness) and how marrow preserves function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ mechanical analogies (syringe, polygon-circle) to explain physiological mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Make use of familiar mechanical devices and geometric reasoning (syringe mixing oil and water, polygon inscribed in a circle) to illustrate how bodily parts function and why their specific arrangements are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose clear, tangible mechanical analogies to make abstract physiological principles understandable to lay readers and to strengthen the inference to contrivance rather than chance.
